Subject: Temporary Shoring and Excavation plan
Comment: SMC 25.09.330 B.6. and SMC 22.170.070 B.2.c. Temporary Excavation and Shoring Sheet A1.2 includes notes that indicate that an ultra block shoring wall will be used, and that the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall continuously monitor installation of the ultra block wall. The subsurface soil conditions include very loose fill and topsoil, underlain by wet, loose silt with organics.  These soil types do not work well with ultra block shoring, which is likely why the use of ultra  block shoring was not included in the 2019 report by Geotech Consultants. The notes on the right side of Sheet A1.2 include a description of slot cuts for this project, a method that was not evaluated in the 2019 report by Geotech Consultants. Upload an addendum to the geotechnical engineering report with methods for excavation of the loose topsoil and fill soil for this project, and update the temporary excavation system accordingly. Make sure the temporary excavation and shoring system includes the existing grade contours, and that the excavation reaches the anticipated bearing depth, which is about 5 feet beneath the existing ground surface. Comment: 3. LATERAL FORCES Page 11 of Geotechnical report states: "Lateral Forces - The capacity of pin pipes to resist lateral loads is very limited and should not be used in design.  Therefore, lateral forces from wind or seismic loading should be resisted by the passive earth pressures acting against the pile caps and below-grade walls or from battered piles (batter no steeper than 3(H):12(V)).  Friction at the base of pile-supported concrete grade beam should be ignored in the design calculations." It appears that battered piles are required to resist lateral forces in the eastward direction (and possibly in the northward direction). Revise plan set to show battered piles, or demonstrate that adequate passive resistance is provided to resist all applicable combinations of lateral loads (lateral earth pressure, seismic, wind, etc.)

Subject: 19 Concrete
Comment: 4. THICKENED SLAB EDGE AT LOWER LEVEL It appears that the thickened slab edge is a cantilever concrete beam. Revise structural as follows:      A. ACI 318-14 section 9.7.2.2 - spacing of bonded longitudinal reinforcement closest to the tension face appears to exceed s given in section 24.3.      B. Reinforcing shown in 1/S4.3 indicates two #8 x 10'-0" longitudinal reinforcing bars at top and bottom of the beam. Subject: 18 Foundations & Retaining Walls
Comment: 5. FOUNDATIONS AT SHEAR WALLS At some locations, holdowns appear to have significant tension demands, compared to the counteracting dead load. Director's Rule 10-2009 allows the use of pin piles for axial compressive loading only (no tension). Some examples are noted below. Provide calculations that demonstrate that the structure shown in plans has adequate dead load to counteract uplift forces due to seismic and wind lateral loads without subjecting pin piles to tensile loading. Use load combinations per SBC 1605 or ASCE 7-16. Revise plans as appropriate.      A. Example 1: HDU8 holdown shown on sheet S2.1 at the north end of the SW6 shear wall on the east side of the AADU bedroom is noted in calculations (page 6 of 67) to have a seismic holdown demand of 8226 lbs. This holdown is anchored to a small foundation shown in section 10/S3.1. Framing span is north-south for most levels, so tributary load to this wall from stories above appears to be very low.       B. Example 2: HDU8 holdowns shown on sheet S2.1 along wall that separates AADU from stair and utility room appears to be anchored to a small foundation shown in section 10/S3.1 that appears to have inadequate flexural and/or shear capacity to distribute concentrated loads (due to shear wall overturning) to engage sufficient counteracting dead load.

Subject: 19 Concrete
Comment: 6. SLAB-ON-GRADE Several details (such as 7/S3.1, 12/S3.1, 1/S4.3) appear to indicate reinforcing bars between critical concrete elements (cantilever slabs, foundations, cantilever beams) and the slab-on-grade. Slab joints, construction joints, and thermal breaks typically provided at non-structural slab on grade would compromise the integrity of this reinforcing and may lead to structural failure. If the intent is to provide structural slab on grade, revise plan set to indicate such, and revise sections and details accordingly. Coordinate with architect the consequences of thermal breaks on structural and energy code requirements.

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Previous cycle correction (by Alan Lee):  Cycle 2: Per your response, SW 202, 102 & 106 uses FTAO methodology but do not show any collectors for shear transfer above and below openings. Please clarify. Current cycle correction:  AWC SDPWS-2015 section 4.3.5.2 Design for force transfer shall be based on a rational analysis. Typically, strength and rigidity of FTAO shear walls relies upon some horizontal axial connectivity of the horizontal panels to the vertical panels, right alongside the top and bottom of wall openings.  The written response letter and accompanying sketch acknowledges these forces, but states that your firm has conducted testing showing that certain shear walls do not need any horizontal collector element right along the top and bottom of openings.  In order for SDCI to accept testing in lieu of calculations, you will need to submit the test results as well as justification that the testing follows SBC protocols.  Therefore, either submit code-justified test findings from an approved agency, or else submit calculations demonstrating how the horizontal forces alongside the top and bottom of openings are transferred between the horizontal and vertical panels of the shear walls.

Comment: This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Stormwater Code.  Drainage Review is required for projects with more than 750 square feet of new and replaced hard surface.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas (not the footprint), driveways, walkways, and parking areas, including gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are considered a hard surface.  Traditional wood decks where the rain can drip through to landscaping or dirt below are not considered as a hard surface.  This project includes new roof area and pervious pavement/pavers that add up to more than 1500 square feet.  Projects with more than 1500sf of new and replaced hard surface are required to provide On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) in accordance with the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual. OSM requirements are described in Section 5.2 (On-site Stormwater Management) of Volume 1 of the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual. The required process for OSM best management practice selection is described in Section 3.3 of Volume 3. The following documents have been prepared to comply with the requirements. These documents are available at http://www.seattle.gov/DPD/codesrules/codes/stormwater/default.htm.  All documents need to use the latest templates available.  Standard details for OSM facilities are available on the Stormwater Code webpage at http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code under "Forms and Documents". You are not required to use the templates, but the submitted plans will need to include all of the relevant information included in the templates.  See Section 8.2 of Volume 1 of the Stormwater Manual for more information on minimum submittal requirements. a) Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Soil Amendment Plan (submitted) b) Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan (submitted) c) On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) Calculator.

Subject: Zoning - SMC 23.54 - Parking, Access, and Solid Waste
Comment: Bike Parking Location and Access. Per SMC 23.54.015.K.2, a). Provide secure locations and arrangements of long-term bicycle parking, with features such as locked rooms or cages and bicycle lockers. The bicycle parking should be installed in a manner that avoids creating conflicts with automobile accesses and driveways. b). For a garage with bicycle parking and motor vehicle parking for more than two dwelling units, provide pedestrian and bicycle access to long-term bicycle parking that is separate from other vehicular entry and egress points or uses the same entry or egress point but has a marked walkway for pedestrians and bicyclists. c).Provide adequate lighting in the bicycle parking area and access routes to it.d.If short-term bicycle parking facilities are not clearly visible from the street or sidewalk or adjacent on-street bicycle facilities, install directional signage in adequate amounts and in highly visible locations in a manner that promotes easy way finding for bicyclists. e).Provide signage to long-term bicycle parking that is oriented to building users. f).Long-term bicycle parking shall be located where bicyclists are not required to carry bicycles on exterior stairs with more than five steps to access the parking. The Director, as a Type I decision, may allow long-term bicycle parking for rowhouse and townhouse development to be accessed by stairs with more than five steps, if the slope of the lot makes access with five or fewer steps infeasible. g).Where practicable, long-term bicycle parking shall include a variety of rack types to accommodate different types of bicycles. h).Install bicycle parking hardware so that it can perform to its manufacturer's specifications and any design criteria promulgated by the Director of the Seattle Department of Transportation, allowing adequate clearance for bicycles and their riders. Please revise and update the plan set as needed

Subject: Zoning - SMC 23.45 - Multifamily
Comment: Gross Floor Area. Per SMC 23.45.510.A, Gross floor area. In multifamily zones, gross floor area includes exterior corridors, breezeways, and stairways that provide building circulation and access to dwelling units or sleeping rooms. Balconies, patios, and decks that are associated with a single dwelling unit or sleeping room and that are not used for common circulation, and ground-level walking paths, are not considered gross floor area. Subject: Zoning
Comment: The provided site plan shows a proposed uncovered porch and steps that encroach into the required front yard.   Per  SMC 23.44.014.C.5, uncovered porches or steps may project into any required yard, if the surface of porches or steps are no higher than 4 feet above existing grade, no closer than 3 feet to any side lot line, and has a width and depth no greater than 6 feet within the required yard.  Though one uncovered, unenclosed porch and/or associated steps are permitted in required yards, portions of the uncovered porch appears to exceed 6 feet in width.  Please revise your proposal and update all drawings so that the  uncovered porch and steps within the required front yard is no higher than 4 feet above existing grade and has a width and depth no greater than 6 feet within the required front yard, as required per SMC 23.44.014.C.5  The planters may be excluded from the height and width calculations for the deck, as they are not part of the deck, but all planters in required yards should be dimensioned on the elevation drawings to demonstrate compliance with SMC 23.44.014.C.10.c

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Correction 1: General Information  This project was reviewed for consistency with SMC 25.09.070: Standards for Vegetation and Impervious Surface Management. The proposed project activities appear to be located within mapped **steep slope environmentally critical areas (ECAs) and their buffers.       Revegetation requirements apply within ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within ECAs and their buffers: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. It appears that the revegetation requirements have not been *met. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set.    Correction 2: Existing Conditions Sheet   1. A0.1, C01, C02,C03: Provide an existing conditions plan. Clearly show the ** steep slope and ECAs and their buffers on the existing conditions plans (like on L1). 2. A01 and arborist report: Trees in ECA's are not categorized by Tier category. Remove references and instead include "ECA".  3. A0.0, A0.1, C01, C02, C03, L1, L2: The land use analysis on A0.0 shows parcel a frequent transit area which requires no parking stalls, but you have proposed 4 parking stalls which in turn requires removal of tree #2, a 33 inch Douglas Fir in a steep slope ECA. The required mitigation sequencing narrative has not been met as avoiding impact the ECA can be avoided by not installing parking stalls in that location [25.09.065.B1a. In addition, the lower priority measures b. through f. shall only be applied if the higher priority measures are infeasible or inapplicable [25.09.065.2]. Subject: Grading season restriction notes
Comment: Repeated Item Please add the following notes to the Temporary Erosion/Sedimentation Control Plan. These notes and requirements are in lieu of establishing a formalized seasonal grading restriction on the project and constitute the customary requirements that would be instituted for a seasonal grading extension:  A site visit from the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall occur during each day of active grading and in the event of significant rainfall which might compromise stabilization measures between November 1 and March 31. The determination of what constitutes significant rainfall is subject to the discretion of the Geotechnical Special Inspector. However, as a minimum standard, the Geotechnical Special Inspector is required to conduct a site visit if more than one-half inch of precipitation occurs on any given day. Any recommendations required to maintain stability of excavations and proper functioning of the sediment/erosion control system provided by the Geotechnical Special Inspector and SDCI personnel shall be implemented immediately. The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide copies of field reports to SDCI Site Development Services Section no later than 48 hours after each inspection. The field reports may be emailed to sdcigeo@seattle.gov. The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide written notice that the site has been stabilized following completion of grading.

Subject: For Projects over 1,500 S.F.
Comment: Sheet C1.2: Repeated Correction: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal: 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Revegetation requirements apply within ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within ECAs: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set. REPEAT CORRECTION: It appears from the survey and aerial imagery that there are trees missing from the plan set as shown on the survey. Please include all tree information for this revegetation correction.  Incorporate information from the vegetation report into the plan set on sheets noted. If it is not in the report, ask the landscape professional to assist. Also, the proposed mitigation planting needs to be on the property where development is being permitted (10031 65th Ave S). The planting can be incorporated in the ECA and elsewhere. The neighbor at 10033 can submit a voluntary restoration request (-TA) record to provide a continuous planting along that slope. Thanks. A. REPEAT A1.0, A1.1, A1.2, CSC, DWC: EXISTING landscape/site plan and table: Provide EXISTING ground coverage conditions. ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within ECAs.  -  Provide total area of impact that requires mitigation: a. Total new hard surface area; b. Total temporary construction disturbance area  c. Use this calculation (a+b=c) for total area of impact that requires mitigation. - Provide a brief description of the EXISTING ground coverage within these areas. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping, blackberry or other invasive species, trees, patio, pathway.  - Show locations of all existing trees to be removed and/or retained. Include a tree table with tree genus, species, common name, DBH (diameter at breast height), driplines, health, and if removed or retained. - Clearly delineate the "Steep Slopes (ECA1)"  and their buffers in the plan set.  - Include a brief summary of the existing ecological functions performed by the ECA on and adjacent to the site. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration.Revegetation (5)

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: B. REPEAT PROPOSED landscape plan and table: Based on existing ground coverage, please show/delineate the PROPOSED mitigation in the form of replanting. Please update site plan and provide the information below: - The location, size, species, quantities and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted per calculation on ECA standard mitigation plan. Tree replacement can be 1:1, shrub multiplier is 0.042 times total area that requires mitigation (see cor. A). https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/TreeVegetationStandardMitigation Plan.pdf - New trees must be two gallon size (4'-6' in height) and shrubs one gallon.  - Planting selections shall be straight NATIVE species suited to specific site conditions/orientation, NO cultivars or hybrids are allowed. - Add a note that areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting. Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: C. REPEAT PROPOSED landscape plan in table: For existing trees proposed for removal SDCI requires that you demonstrate the use of required mitigation sequencing in the project development phase (SMC 25.09.065.B.1). These required steps are meant to find the least environmentally-damaging practicable alternative to achieve a project need to construct the updates you are proposing and trees you are proposing for removal.  Include items a. through f.in a table with responses to each. Additionally, show how you have considered of these items in order per SMC 25.09.065.B2. which states that the lower priority measures (b. through f.) shall only be applied if the higher priority measure (a.) is infeasible or inapplicable. Mitigation sequencing must be undertaken in the order of priority listed.    a. Avoiding the impact altogether by not taking a certain action or parts of an action; b. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts; c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment; d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations; e. Compensating for the impact by replacing, enhancing, or providing substitute resources or environments; and f. Monitoring the impact and the compensation projects undertaken under subsection 25.09.065.B.1.e and taking appropriate corrective measures.

Subject: Seismic Site Class and Slope Stability Analysis
Comment: The uploaded geotechnical report assumed Site Class D to determine seismic coefficients. To categorize the site as Site Class D, please demonstrate one of the following criteria: a) Shear wave velocity for the top 100 ft is between 600 and 1,200 ft/s. b) SPT-N blow counts for the top 100 ft are between 15 and 50 per foot. c) Undrained shear strength for the top 100 ft is between 1,000 and 2,000 lb/ft². The subsurface explorations presented in the uploaded geotechnical report lack sufficient detail to determine the site class. As per Section 11.4.3 of ASCE 7-16, when soil properties are not known in sufficient detail to determine the site class, Site Class D is selected as the default site class, and the value of Fa shall not be less than 1.2 and site modified peak ground acceleration (PGAM) of 0.648 g should be used in slope stability analysis. Revise the seismic design parameters and update the slope stability analysis using site modified PGA.ECA GeoTech (4)

Subject: Slope Stability Analysis
Comment: Please provide an addendum to the geotechnical report that includes the revised slope stability analysis, input parameters (including infiltration rate and revised seismic coefficients), and analysis results, addressing the following comments: a) The reviewer believes the test pits in the original geotechnical report are insufficient to establish the soil profile. Please have a geotechnical engineer provide a detailed explanation of how the soil profile used for the slope stability analysis was depicted. b) A cohesion value of 100 psf was applied to the Advance Outwash. However, the reviewer believes that cohesion should not be considered for Advance Outwash. c) The entry and exit points used in the slope stability analysis are unclear. Please clearly identify and illustrate the entry and exit points, ensuring they are sufficient to capture the most critical slip surfaces. d) Clearly depict the groundwater table both before and after infiltration. e) Include the building load and any associated surcharge load in the analysis.

The proposed project activities appear to be located within mapped **steep slope and potential landslide prone environmentally critical areas (ECAs) and their buffers.       Revegetation requirements apply within **steep slope and potential landslide prone ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within these ECAs and their buffers: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. It appears that the revegetation requirements have not been *met. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set.    ** steep slope and potential slide ECAs *  addressed   Correction 2: Existing Conditions Sheet  (existing site plan w/o improvements) 1. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping (vegetation species), blackberry or other invasive species, tree species, patio, pathway, driveway, stairway, etc. Calculate the area in square footage and show this on the existing conditions plan.  3. Show locations of all existing trees located within and adjacent to the disturbance area consistently across all plan view sheets. Include a tree table with genus, species, common name, DSH (diameter at standard height), dripline diameter and if trees/vegetation are proposed to remain or be removed. Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list of the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ** steep slope and potential landslide prone ECA. Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: If you intend to use the existing side sewer/s, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewers were installed prior to 2004.  The necessary forms may be submitted prior to drainage approval of the building permit application, or a very clear, prominent boxed note added to the Civil Site Plan that the existing side sewer must be evaluated and certified prior to the connection to the side sewer.  Side Sewer Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer.  In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the line must either be lined, or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. If, at this time, you do not intend to use an existing side sewer, please show and label a new connection to the sewer main.  This will also require further correction items and plan sheet notes with my next review.  The Side Sewer Evaluation and Certification Form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/SideSewerEvaluationCertification.pdf On the DWC Plan, please add a prominent boxed note that says, “Per Side Sewer Code 21.16.240, the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either Pressure Tested or Lined all the way to the public mainline in the street. ”

Subject: Tree Replacement Requirements (SMC 25.11.090)
Comment: Removal of Tree 4 must meet tree replacement requirements. Tier 4 trees do not have to be replaced. Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 trees removed in association with development must be replaced by one or more new trees designed to result, upon maturity, in a canopy cover that is at least roughly proportional to the canopy cover prior to tree removal. Replacement trees must also be native and/or culturally significant, and resilient to climate change (SMC 25.11.090.C.2). Please refer to Director ’s Rule 12-2023 for more information about tree replacement requirements. Please note that the GreenFactor Plant list referenced in this rule only lists bioretention trees, which are only appropriate in wet areas. Please choose a drought-tolerant species. Required right-of-way trees do not count for Tier 3 replacement.  Thuja occidentalis planted as a hedge for screening also do not count for Tier 3 replacement.  Feel free to email me with species selection questions.

The free-draining aggregate surrounding each paver shall meet the requirements of the storage reservoir or the leveling course aggregates. The minimum required spacing between pavers is estimated by multiplying the required area by 2 and dividing by the perimeter of the paver per the following equation:  Spacing (between pavers) = 2 X Paver Area (square inches) X (10 percent) / Perimeter Length of Paver (inches).  Please clarify on the plan how the proposed PPS is meeting the minimum requirements above.5 (1)

Comment: Sheet A01: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer*. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*. *Note: for Infiltration testing and plan preparation clarification for detached accessory dwelling units (DADUs) and additions with less than 1,500 sf of new plus replaced hard surface on lots with No Off-site Point of Discharge:   The applicant is allowed to perform the infiltration testing unless otherwise determined by the Director.   If the applicant chooses (in lieu of a licensed professional) to conduct the infiltration testing, the applicant shall conduct the Small PIT (rather than the Simple Infiltration Test).   The test shall be documented with the Pilot Infiltration Test Checklist and a minimum 0.25 in/hr measured soil infiltration rate must be demonstrated.   Drywells shall be sized, at a minimum, per Appendix E-10 - Drywell Sizing Tables of the  Seattle Stormwater Manual.   The applicant is allowed to prepare the drainage control plan unless otherwise determined by the Director.Drainage (2)

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: AWC SDPWS 4.1.3 and ASCE 7-16 12.1 – Member strength and deformation compatibility.  Detail 2/S7.0 shows that shear wall boundary holdowns of upper levels are allowed to develop only into the shear wall of the level below (i.e. the upper wall ’s right side boundary element does not have aligned holdowns/studs continuous full-building height straight down into the foundation).  It is understood that the intent is that the shear wall at the level below distributes the upper level boundary holdown reaction outward to its own boundary members in shear.  As a horizontally-spanning member, this shear will also be accompanied by flexure (i.e. the lower wall acts as a deep beam).  The beam ’s moment and deflection diagrams would be those corresponding to the shear diagram shown on calculation page 473.  For this deep beam design approach, please justify that all elements are structurally adequate considering simultaneous forces and displacement compatibility, as follows: 1) To develop the intended resisting beam action, the lower shear wall will have to flex upward.  It does not appear, however, that there is a connection at the base of the lower wall or anywhere below it that is meant to “give” to allow this deflected beam shape to occur.  Clarify what is the mechanism that deforms/releases to allow the lower wall ’s deflected shape (and that such release does not result in a required load path having inadequate strength). 2) Initially until the lower wall deflects enough to carry the load horizontally through the plywood by beam action, it appears that the upper wall ’s boundary element in the lower wall will have the following load path:  the boundary element will pull up the lower wall ’s sheathing, such that the bottom of the sheathing will pull up its sheathing nailing which will pull the sill plate upwards in cross-grain bending, the sill plate will pull up on the rim board through its connectors, which will pull up the foundation sill plate through its connectors, and so on down all stories to the foundation (i.e. this is the initial de facto holdown load path).  Justify that all unreleased elements from the lower shear wall ’s sheathing on downward are adequate to resist the initial uplift force (in combination with other simultaneous forces) until the deep beam action engages. 3) For the flexure of the deep beam, it appears that the lower wall ’s top and bottom plates or rim joist potentially act as flanges (horizontal chords) of the beam (whether intended or not).  Within the calculations, clarify which elements are loaded by the flexure of the lower shearwall.  For elements that receive load as chords, demonstrate that all simultaneous loads within them and their connectors are accounted for (such as shear wall shear, horizontal shear flow for the beam action, external drag strut forces in the double top plate, etc.). 4) Ensure that any justifying calculations utilize code-required load combinations (such as .6D+.7E, if applicable).         ALL SCHEDULE

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Original correction:  AWC SDPWS 4.1.3 and ASCE 7-16 12.1 – Member strength and deformation compatibility.  Detail 2/S7.0 shows that shear wall boundary holdowns of upper levels are allowed to develop only into the shear wall of the level below (i.e. the upper wall ’s right side boundary element does not have aligned holdowns/studs continuous full-building height straight down into the foundation).  It is understood that the intent is that the shear wall at the level below distributes the upper level boundary holdown reaction outward to its own boundary members in shear.  As a horizontally-spanning member, this shear will also be accompanied by flexure (i.e. the lower wall acts as a deep beam).  The beam ’s moment and deflection diagrams would be those corresponding to the shear diagram shown on calculation page 473.  For this deep beam design approach, please justify that all elements are structurally adequate considering simultaneous forces and displacement compatibility, as follows: 1) To develop the intended resisting beam action, the lower shear wall will have to flex upward.  It does not appear, however, that there is a connection at the base of the lower wall or anywhere below it that is meant to “give” to allow this deflected beam shape to occur.  Clarify what is the mechanism that deforms/releases to allow the lower wall ’s deflected shape (and that such release does not result in a required load path having inadequate strength). 2) Initially until the lower wall deflects enough to carry the load horizontally through the plywood by beam action, it appears that the upper wall ’s boundary element in the lower wall will have the following load path:  the boundary element will pull up the lower wall ’s sheathing, such that the bottom of the sheathing will pull up its sheathing nailing which will pull the sill plate upwards in cross-grain bending, the sill plate will pull up on the rim board through its connectors, which will pull up the foundation sill plate through its connectors, and so on down all stories to the foundation (i.e. this is the initial de facto holdown load path).  Justify that all unreleased elements from the lower shear wall ’s sheathing on downward are adequate to resist the initial uplift force (in combination with other simultaneous forces) until the deep beam action engages. 3) For the flexure of the deep beam, it appears that the lower wall ’s top and bottom plates or rim joist potentially act as flanges (horizontal chords) of the beam (whether intended or not).  Within the calculations, clarify which elements are loaded by the flexure of the lower shearwall.  For elements that receive load as chords, demonstrate that all simultaneous loads within them and their connectors are accounted for (such as shear wall shear, horizontal shear flow for the beam action, external drag strut forces in the double top plate, etc.). 4) Ensure that any justifying calculations utilize code-required load combinations (such as .6D+.7E, if applicable). Current cycle correction:  SDCI is appreciative that you are providing a technical justification with calculations to support your position, as this is the best path toward resolving the deformation compatibility concern raised in our corrections.  Because of the uniqueness of this topic, you may email to the reviewer your follow-up response to this correction in-between review cycles, so as to help resolve it more quickly.  Following are some broader responses to your written responses: 1) The reason that SDCI does not view this detail the same as a flexible horizontal diaphragm is that a shearwall is restrained along its whole bottom edge.  If it were not, then we agree that it would be analogous to a horizontal flexible diaphragm (which typically does not have restraint to flexure along its far edge). 2) Your response mentioned that in a normally loaded shear wall, any incidental pulling up on the sill plate by the sheathing is ignored.  The difference to SDCI is that the testing that SDPWS shear wall tables are based upon accounted for the extent of that behavior that is caused by the shear wall resisting horizontal loading at the top of the shear wall.  Those tests, however, did not account for the simultaneous additional uplift from a concentrated vertical load introduced within the length of the shear wall. 3) Regarding the code sections mentioned in the original correction (AWC SDPWS 4.1.3 and ASCE 7-16 12.1), your response says that this portion of ASCE 7 does not support our concern.  SDCI disagrees as we do not see it stated therein that these code sections are limited to just the scenario you describe (gravity elements accommodating lateral displacement).  Within the subsections of 12.1 are general requirements that building elements shall be adequate to withstand forces and deformations they are subject to, which are the questions we are raising about this detail. 4) Based upon mechanics of materials, it is SDCI ’s position that the shear resistance of the wall that is being relied upon to carry the interior uplift force outward to the wall ends cannot be developed without the shear wall experiencing corresponding flexure (same as a beam that supports an interior point load).  In this detail, the beam (shear wall) is not being allowed to experience that necessary upward flexure because it is restrained all along its bottom edge.  Therefore, the upward load will not follow the more flexible shear path outward to the wall ends as you desire, but is instead being translated straight down through the sheathing into the sill plate.  We are concerned that this rigid load path downward will cause nails to tear out at the bottom of the sheathing, and sill plate cross grain bending, and uplift on the sill plate nails, and uplift on elements below. Assumedly, none of these elements were designed to carry this vertical load in addition to the forces they must resist for the shear wall ’s horizontal load. Due to length of this correction, see separate correction herein requesting specific further justification about the analysis you have provided. )

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Original correction:  AWC SDPWS 4.1.3 and ASCE 7-16 12.1 – Member strength and deformation compatibility.  Detail 2/S7.0 shows that shear wall boundary holdowns of upper levels are allowed to develop only into the shear wall of the level below (i.e. the upper wall ’s right side boundary element does not have aligned holdowns/studs continuous full-building height straight down into the foundation) … Current cycle correction:  Your response mentions that you assume the wall ’s double top plate and single bottom plate act as chords for flexural deflection associated with this vertical uplift load.  SDCI agrees with this approach as it is very consistent with the beam analogy that SDPWS prescribes for diaphragms and shear walls.  Therefore, if the wall were not restrained along the base from deflecting upward, we are in agreement that the wall’s deflection upward is analogous to a horizontal diaphragm deflection.  Please address the following for the calculations and technical justification you have provided in response to this correction: 1) Any pulling upward on the base of the wall with this additional interior reaction is beyond the scope of the testing that is the basis of the SDPWS shear wall assemblies.  Therefore, SDCI is requesting those uplift forces be added to the forces that base elements are simultaneously experiencing from the conventional shear wall forces.  Because your approach is to instead show that upward deflection is minimal, provide technical justification what is the maximum amount of calculated upward shear wall deflection that is inconsequential to the strength and deformation of the restraining elements that are along the shear wall base (i.e. panel bottom nails and elements below). 2) For the FEM modeling submitted, clarify which program was used and also upload printed model input and output for further review. 3) Justify that the upward deflection modeling accounts for all contributing sources of deflection prescribed in SDPWS 4.2.3.   Also, please provide a hand calculation of the upward deflection using the formula in this code section (for comparison to the FEM model). 4) Clarify how the FEM input models the wood plates that serve as chords along the top and the bottom of the shear walls.  Because your drawings do not prohibit laps in the double top plates from occurring along the tops of shear walls, demonstrate that the model assumes only a single continuous top plate acting as a tension chord. 5) Clarify the shear wall length and height that is used in the upward deflection calculation and ensure that the loads and dimensions are the most conservative that could occur on this project.

Please address the following: 1) The submitted results for shear wall panel B (page 90 of the supplemental calculations) shows uniform net uplift at the bottom of the shear wall that appears to be up to 200 plf in places.  As the previous correction cycles requested in significant detail, submit calculations showing that all elements from the shear wall bottom nails on downward can withstand these uplift forces concurrently with their other simultaneous loads. 2) The analysis appears to be unconservative in some ways compared to what is allowed by the drawings, as described in items 3 through 5 below.  Also, the calculations for bottom-most shear wall panel D (referenced on calculation page 70) have not been provided - please submit.  If all of this is ultimately addressed, it appears that the loads mentioned in item 1 may be even higher than they are now. 3) The third column of the shear wall schedule on drawing S7.0 appears to allow the wall to be sheathed with either plywood or OSB.  Either update the drawings to not allow plywood sheathing, or else update these calculations to use the more conservative plywood values for Ga. 4) Calculation pages such as 94 assume the double top plates are DF but the drawings seem to allow Hem-Fir for them.  Either update these calculations to use HF properties for all elements that the drawings allow HF, or else update the drawings to specify DF where used in the calculations. 5) Page 8 of the response states that double top plates shall not have splices in them above shear walls per detail 2/S7.0, however the nailing schedule on drawing S1.0 appears to allow this.  Even if a note were to be added to 2/S7.0 expressly disallowing top plate splices above shear walls, the detail already has a note disallowing top plate splices over headers.  It does not seem realistic that 2x lumber can be obtained in 26 to 30 feet lengths as would be needed for these buildings if lap splices are allowed over neither the headers or shear walls (the concern with this is that splices will have to be added in construction out of necessity, which would invalidate the current assumption in the calculations). 6) Per SDPWS 4.3.7.1, shear wall nails only require 3/8 ” edge distance for a typical laterally loaded shear wall.  Given the desire to also load them in uplift such that nail loads are toward the panel end (i.e. sheathing in tension), it appears the panel end distance for affected nails should be increased to prevent sheathing tear out.  See SDPWS Table C12.1.6.6 that recommends up to 15d edge distance for this scenario.

Comment: Original correction:  Detail 12/S7.1 -  Please provide intermittent full-depth perpendicular blocking alongside the drag joist, or else otherwise justify that the top of the shearwall will not hinge out-of-plane due to gravity loads from above in combination with lateral loads acting either parallel or perpendicular to the wall plane. 2nd cycle correction:  The written response is that the detail is adequate without any blocking due to low gravity loads on these walls.  Reviewer concurs that on this project the gravity loads from above are low, thus the P-delta from gravity loads will not contribute much to wall hinging.  Therefore, neglecting any effect from gravity loads, please address the original correction for just the lateral loads acting perpendicular to the wall plane, as follows: 1) Demonstrate that the load path without intermittent blocking is adequate for out-of-plane wind loads acting on an exterior wall (for example, where the exterior wall at grid 2 attaches to the 2nd floor). Please also address this for detail 12/S7.1 as was requested in the previous cycle corrections.

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Original correction:  There does not appear to be a vertical lateral load resisting system for the end of the penthouse roof that is along grid 5 (for units C and D), and along grid 1 (for units A and B).  Please clarify how lateral load resistance is provided for this end of these roof diaphragms, or justify that the roofs comply with AWC SDPWS-2021 4.2.6 for open front diaphragms. 2nd cycle correction:  The written response is that the penthouses have SW-1 shear walls.  The wall lines mentioned in the original correction, however, have significant windows within them such that there is not a solid shear wall.  The lack of a shear wall here may lead to racking of these walls under design lateral loads.  Provide calculations showing how both penthouses have code-compliant lateral load paths, considering these open wall ends.  One potential solution used by some engineers is to provide cantilevered posts as the lateral load resisting system for that wall (designed to the appropriate seismic R-value per ASCE 7-16 Table 12.2-1). Current cycle correction:  This correction has mostly been resolved by the addition of the vertically cantilevered 5.25 PSL posts for both penthouses.  Detail 3/S7.2 has been added to show how vertical and horizontal continuity of various structural elements are maintained for units C and D.  Please address the following: 1) Clarify on the plans if detail 3/S7.2 is also applicable for the penthouse at units A and B, or if it has different detailing. 2) While detail 3/S7.2 shows helpful hatching for the full height PSL posts, there are some possible reasons the contractor will provide a break in these posts at the roof level.  This is because the plans have separate callouts for the posts at both the roof and penthouse roof levels, and also there are roof level girder trusses needing gravity support by these posts at units C and D.  To alleviate these concerns, please add a note to the drawings explicitly stating the posts shall be continuous full height from third floor to penthouse roof, and also a note that the truss designer shall design these roof-level girder trusses as face-mounted to these continuous posts.

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Original correction:  At grid C of both buildings between the stairwell openings the drawings show structural walls full height of the building.  The calculations show that these walls are being designed as shear walls that collect load from each story.  Please address the following: 1) Clarify how horizontal load is collected from the floor/roof diaphragms into the portions of the shear walls that are between the stair wells. 2) For these walls between the stairwells, clarify in the calculations that the framing specified on the drawings will result in a complete load path for resisting their out-of-plane seismic loads. 2nd cycle correction (item numbers correspond to item numbers of previous cycle correction): 1) The written response is that the loads from the diaphragms are carried into these walls through continuous top plates.  For these walls that have no floor framing into them on either side, provide details showing your intent that at each diaphragm level a continuous top plate shall be provided at the same height (and connected to) the top plate that supports the floor/roof beyond. 2) The written response is that the out-of-plane wall load is only 2 psf.  In lieu of justification otherwise, however, it appears that these walls will also be loaded out-of-plane by the seismic weight of the stairs.  Provide calculations as requested in the original correction. Current cycle correction:  The written response shows Figure 12.10.1 of ASCE7-16.  Reviewer agrees that figure is analogous to these grid C walls.   Please address the following (item numbers correspond to item numbers of previous cycle correction): 1) As requested in the previous cycle, provide a detail at each floor level showing the intended framing.  Reviewer understands that the intent is the studs are not continuous vertically past floor levels and instead there is some continuous horizontal framing (such as double top plates or a beam) that will distribute the loads collected from each floor within the length of the grid C shear wall.  This intent, however, is not clear from the current lack of detailing. 2) The submitted calculations do indeed show that the out-of-plane loads on these walls is not very high.  Even with these relatively small loads, however, the horizontal spans are up to 13.25 ft, which is pretty long for a wall double top plate (and for calculation purposes, the double top plate is effectively more like only a single 2x, since splices are allowed in it).  Therefore, provide a calculation showing that whatever continuous horizontal element is provided in the wall length is adequate for out-of-plane loads.  In these cases, engineers often find they need to provide a continuous beam in lieu of rim blocking the full length of the wall along diaphragm stair openings to resist the out-of-plane loads.

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Original correction:  Drawings S2.2 and S2.4 show trusses supporting the shear walls of the penthouse.   Please provide the following information on the drawings for the prefab truss manufacturer to include in their design: 1) If any trusses are required to drag horizontal loads from the penthouse shearwalls into the roof diaphragm, specify that horizontal axial load. 2) ASCE 7-16 12.3.3.3 -  Specify the seismic vertical overturning loads, amplified by overstrength, that will occur at shearwall ends; and also overturning wind loads. 2nd cycle correction:  The written response states there are no drag loads or overturning loads acting on the supporting trusses.  Reviewer is unable to find where the penthouse lateral loads design is provided in the calculation package, but can see in the submitted wind calculations that the sum of leeward and windward loads at the penthouse height are almost 30 psf.  From this, the reviewer calculates about 2.5 kips of horizontal wind load reaction at each end of the penthouse plus the additional net wind uplift acting on the roof.  For the walls at the north and south ends of each penthouse, it appears this will result in a net upward/downward force of 1 kip or higher.  Please address the following for both buildings ’ penthouses: 1) Provide wind and seismic calculations of the penthouse to determine overturning reactions at the end walls.  Provide holdowns as determined necessary using SBC load combinations. 2) As requested in the original correction, state on the drawings the upward and downward wind and seismic overturning reactions that are acting on the trusses (for the truss designer to use in their own load combinations).  State that the truss design shall amplify overturning seismic loads by overstrength. 3) Demonstrate that the penthouse wind and seismic lateral loads have been included in the overall building design. Current correction:  Supplemental calculations have been provided and holdown seismic forces have been added to the drawings.  Please address the following: 1) Holdowns have been added to the penthouse of units A and B.  Also specify the holdowns on the penthouse of units C and D. 2) As previously requested, state on the drawings for the truss engineer both the wind and seismic vertical forces at the shear wall ends and clarify that these overturning forces can occur either upward or downward. 3) Confirm whether or not the 1350 lbs vertical seismic force that is currently specified on the drawings includes the overstrength factor (as is required for the truss design). 4) Provide a detail on the drawings clarifying how the strap holdowns shall be attached to the trusses.  Alternatively, add notes clarifying what the truss engineer shall provide as part of their truss design to receive the holdown strap. 5) Regarding item 3 of the previous cycle correction, supplemental calculation page 44 shows the roof level forces with penthouse lateral loads included.  That graphic, however, does not appear to include the forces from the penthouse ’s wall along grid D.  Update the graphic to include those forces. 6) Even though the original design calculations (such as page 9) showed applied global lateral loads that include the penthouse level, it appears from this updated graphic of roof level forces that penthouse lateral loads may have been omitted from the building ’s original design calculations.  For example, the roof level shear wall loads applied to grids 1 and 3 of units A and B (shown on pages 24 and 39 of the original calculations) appear to not include these penthouse loads.  In lieu of justification that the original building designs did include penthouse lateral loads, submit updated calculations showing the building designs do account for them.

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Original correction:  Detail 12/S7.1 specifies A35 connectors at 24 inches o.c.  Please justify this will be adequate capacity at grid 2 on drawing S2.3 to transfer shear from the 2nd floor diaphragm to the shear wall below (assuming hem fir framing as is allowed by the general notes). 2nd cycle correction:  The written response is that the shear wall along grid 2 need only carry 48 plf.  This is an unusually low force for a bottom level wall.  Looking back at the original calculations, this wall design appears to not include the load from the two stories above plus penthouse (i.e. from the shearwalls at level 1, which appear may add up to 10 kips additional load).  Furthermore, the grid 2 reaction will increase beyond the input loads due to it being the interior reaction point for a cantilevered diaphragm (using beam statics).  Please address the following: 1) Update the lateral load calculations to account for all of these forces that utilize grid 2 shear walls, and verify that all elements in the load path are adequately designed. 2) Confirm that the calculations do not have any other shear wall lines where the upper level wall forces have not been included in the lower level shear wall design. Current cycle correction:  Supplemental calculation pages 96 and 97 have been submitted in response to the correction.  Please address the following: 1) The supplemental calculations state that E=8152 lbs at the grid 2 wall, however it appears that the load here might be substantially more.  According to original calculation page 24, the total seismic loads for the shear walls above (at grid 1) is 8259 lbs.  Then it appears another 600 lbs should be added from the penthouse (see other correction herein).  Summing moments about grid 5, it therefore appears the grid 1 walls above would cause the following reaction at grid 2: (8259 + 600)x(30 ’/24’) = 11074 lbs.  Then the seismic forces from the level 2 diaphragm and self-wt of the wall should be added (E=1552 lbs total per original calculation page 37).  Therefore, it appears that the sum of forces in the grid 2 walls are 11074 + 1552 lbs = 12626 lbs.  If this is accurate, then the shear wall size should be increased and the A35 connectors spaced closer together.   Reviewer did not check the stated wind load of 12340 lbs but assumes it needs to be increased similarly.  Provide updated calculations. 2) In lieu of acceptable justification otherwise, revise the A35 connector capacity on calculation page 97 to use the value for hem-fir (475 lbs) as was mentioned in the cycle 1 correction.  3) If the grid 2 wall will actually experience higher loads as described in item 1, then provide updated calculations showing that the grid 2 wall holdowns are adequate and that the interior footings provide adequate upward and downward resistance using code-required load combinations.

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePerme ablePavement.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: General Information / Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Subject: Grading season restriction notes
Comment: Please add the following notes to the Temporary Erosion/Sedimentation Control Plan. These notes and requirements are in lieu of establishing a formalized seasonal grading restriction on the project and constitute the customary requirements that would be instituted for a seasonal grading extension:   A site visit from the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall occur during each day of active grading and in the event of significant rainfall which might compromise stabilization measures between November 1 and March 31. The determination of what constitutes significant rainfall is subject to the discretion of the Geotechnical Special Inspector. However, as a minimum standard, the Geotechnical Special Inspector is required to conduct a site visit if more than one-half inch of precipitation occurs on any given day. Any recommendations required to maintain stability of excavations and proper functioning of the sediment/erosion control system provided by the Geotechnical Special Inspector and SDCI personnel shall be implemented immediately.  The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide copies of field reports to SDCI Site Development Services Section no later than 48 hours after each inspection. The field reports must be uploaded to the Geotechnical Special Inspection Account on the permit portal associated with this building permit application. The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide written notice that the site has been stabilized following completion of grading.ECA GeoTech (6)

Subject: DADUs & ADD/ALT less than 1500 S.F.
Comment: Sheet DWC: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer*. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*. *Note: for Infiltration testing and plan preparation clarification for detached accessory dwelling units (DADUs) and additions with less than 1,500 sf of new plus replaced hard surface on lots with No Off-site Point of Discharge:   The applicant is allowed to perform the infiltration testing unless otherwise determined by the Director.   If the applicant chooses (in lieu of a licensed professional) to conduct the infiltration testing, the applicant shall conduct the Small PIT (rather than the Simple Infiltration Test).   The test shall be documented with the Pilot Infiltration Test Checklist and a minimum 0.25 in/hr measured soil infiltration rate must be demonstrated.   Drywells shall be sized, at a minimum, per Appendix E-10 - Drywell Sizing Tables of the  Seattle Stormwater Manual.   The applicant is allowed to prepare the drainage control plan unless otherwise determined by the Director.Drainage (5)

Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.44 – Single-Family Residential
Comment: The plans propose eave and gutter projections on the south side of the proposed DADU that falls within the required rear yard that appear to extend 2 ’ south of the DADU wall line. Per Table A for SMC 23.44.401, letter i, footnote 4, external architectural details with no living area, such as chimneys, eaves, cornices, and columns, may project no closer than 3 feet from any lot line. Update the plans to dimension the distance between the edge of the projection(s) and the south property line of the projections that are within the rear yard. Note, only architectural projections that fall within the side yard may apply the standard in SMC 23.44.014.C.4.e.

Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.44 – Single-Family Residential
Comment: The plans propose to convert/rebuild and expand the footprint of the existing accessory structure to establish a DADU. Part of the DADU is proposed to encroach upon the required rear yard at a distance less than 5 ’ from the south side lot line. Per Table A for SMC 23.44.014, letter i, a detached accessory dwelling unit may be located within a required rear yard if it is not within 5 feet of any lot line, unless the lot line is adjacent to an alley, in which case a detached accessory dwelling unit may be located at that lot line. Update the plans to dimension the distance between the proposed DADU that is within the required rear yard and the south side lot line to demonstrate compliance with Table A for SMC 23.44.041, letter i.

Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.44 – Single-Family Residential
Comment: It is unclear if the proposed DADU encroaches slightly into the required north side yard. Per Table A for SMC 23.44.041, Letter H, a detached accessory dwelling unit may not be located within the side yard required by subsection 23.44.014.B except as provided in subsection 23.44.014.C.3 or 23.44.014.C.4, and footnote 4 of Table A for SMC 23.44.041. Additionally SDCI DR 4-2019 states, “for purposes of yard or setback standards, measurement shall be taken to the outside surface of the building foundation rather than to exterior finishing such as siding, provided that the finishes extend no more than 6 inches into a required yard or setback ”. Update the plans to demonstrate the proposed DADU is outside of the required north side yard in accordance with Table A for SMC 23.44.041, Letter H and SDCI DR 4-2019 (https://www.seattle.gov/dpd/codes/dr/DR2019-4.pdf).

Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.44 – Single-Family Residential
Comment: The plans do not appear to include gross floor area (GFA) calculations for the proposed detached accessory dwelling unit (DADU) and the GFA diagrams appear to be incomplete. Update the plans to include GFA calculations to demonstrate the DADU does not exceed the allowed 1,000 square feet GFA per Table A for SMC 23.44.041, letter f. Please take note of the areas that are excluded from GFA per letter f in Table A for SMC 23.44.041. GFA should be measured from the interior face of the exterior walls (see Director ’s Rule 4-2019, https://www.seattle.gov/dpd/codes/dr/DR2019-4.pdf ). There is no floor area figure provided for the lower level. It also appears that the interior wall between the garage and living area is being completely exempt from GFA. This shared wall area should be split between the two areas (garage vs living area). Additionally, it appears that parts of the upper floor are not counted toward GFA due to floor to ceiling height of less than 7 ’. Please verify the actual amount of chargeable floor area at the upper level and update the GFA diagrams as necessary to show which portions of the upper level are chargeable vs exempt from GFA. Provide floor to ceiling height measurements for the upper level to substantiate the amount of chargeable floor area at that level of this structure for all areas being exempt. Update the plans to include GFA calculations for both floors of the proposed DADU that demonstrate compliance with Table A for SMC 23.44.041, letter f.
