Subject: PE Evaluation & Certification Required
Comment: If you intend to reuse existing side sewer, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewer/s were installed prior to 2004.   SS Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer. In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the side sewer must either be lined or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. Please add  a very clear, boxed note added to the Drainage and Wastewater Control Plan that  the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either rehabilitated (i.e. lined) or pressure tested all the way to the public mainline in the street.  The completed Evaluation and Certification form must be submitted to the inspector during construction.  The form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/dpd/permits/permittypes/sidesewer/default.htm

General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Additionally, single-family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must also implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference / when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  Please ensure that you are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates (when applicable and if not already included in the complete plan set) and/or standard plan notes.  Please note that even if drainage review is not required, a completed Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan is required to be included in the complete plan set when there is any ground disturbance.  As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable.  As part of the complete plan set, please submit the following: A completed Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan.  This sheet is required anytime there will be ground disturbance of any kind onsite. A completed Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan including the Site and Drainage Control Summary from On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator.  And when applicable, as a separate upload, please also submit a PDF of the entire completed On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator for review and retention. If either building has walls or projections that are less than 5 feet from the line (not 5 ft from each other), show 1-hour protection per SRC Table R302.1(1) on the plans. A1.0] Note, if the scope of work includes alterations to the existing SFR a separate permit application is required. If this is the case, please obtain a record number for the SFR permit application and clearly indicate on plan the scope of work under the other record number. The aerial for this property appears to show eaves on the West side of the roof. However, the 5 ft separation requirement is measured to the imaginary line (fire separation distance), not the distance between structures. I should have also clarified the following on my prior comments: The East DADU wall is shown with 1'-2" separation distance. This wall requires 1-hr rated construction and no openings would be allowed. The imaginary line could jog where the garage vehicle door is located to allow both the door opening and the wall to be unrated for this portion. Also, revise the plan note to clarify the SFR eaves, if any, are min. 5 ft from the imaginary line. Alternatively, revise the imaginary line and show compliance with table R302.1(1) for rated wall construction, projections, and opening percentages. Feel free to contact me by phone or email if you have questions prior to the response submittal.Ordinance Structural (1)

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Correction A: General Information  This project was reviewed for consistency with SMC 25.09.070: Standards for Vegetation and Impervious Surface Management. The proposed project activities appear to be located within mapped **potential landslide prone environmentally critical areas (ECAs) and their buffers.       Revegetation requirements apply within ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within potential landslide prone ECAs and their buffers: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. It appears that the revegetation requirements have not been *met. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set.    1. CSC, DWC: Add tree identifers on trees and note "See existing tree table on A0.1 or A0.3".  Correction B: Existing Conditions (A0.1, A0.3) 1. A0.1: Update tree schedule to remove Tier category number for trees and instead include "ECA" as trees in ECAs are not categorized by tier categories. This was done on A0.3. 2. A0.3: Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list of the  ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ** potential landslide prone ECA. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration (SMC 25.09.065.C.2.a).    Correction C: Project Impacts  A0.3, A0.4 and A0.5 show different calculations, update to follow the rule below. It appears the total should be closer to 5604 SF as noted on site plan. [25.09.065.C.2] Update to include on one sheet only to determine the total area of impact that requires mitigation using the calculation (a+b=c):  a. Total new hard surface area  b. Total temporary construction disturbance area including all construction-related activities including, but not limited to construction access, staging area, temporary excavation, and areas of tree/vegetation removal.   c. Total area of impact that requires mitigation in the form of replanting (use cor. Item 3 for multiplier of new shrubs required). Calculations should only include areas within property lines, as we cannot approve information on the adjacent property.    Correction D:  Proposed Mitigation  1. A0.5: On the mitigation plan, show the location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted and those existing to be retained on site. Use the ECA standard mitigation plan as a guide only.   a. Shrub quantities can be determined by using multiplier 0.042 times the total area of impact that requires mitigation.   b. Tree replacement quantities can be 1:1 or alternatively use an adjusted tree multiplier of 0.01 as the ECA standard mitigation plan multiplier results in an excessive number of trees. The goal is to provide a layered canopy. Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan    References to help you choose native plants:   King County Native Plant Guide: Plant list - Native Plant Guide (kingcounty.gov)   WSU Native Plant Guide:WSU PNW Plants    2. Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list, an analysis of how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA.    3. Add note stating:  a. Planting selections shall be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation, no cultivars or hybrids are allowed.  b. New trees must be 4-6 feet in height and shrubs one-gallon size.  c. Areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting. Mulch, such as wood chips, should be added to a 3 ” thickness over the entire planting area without covering the stems of plants. Revegetation (1)

If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: Sheet DWC: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). Comment: On the DWC Plan – sheet C1.1, if applicable, please clearly show and label the perimeter foundation/footing drain discharge lines ( “FD” or “DRN ”) being routed directly to and passing through a catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer connection to the combined sewer main.   Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.E.1 “Water collected by subsurface drains shall pass through a catch basin before discharge to a public system or watercourse …”  See also, Table C in Section VII.D.   Catch basins for footing drains must have a 2 ’ deep minimum sump and a sump volume of 2 cubic feet.  This must be called out on the DWC Plan. Footing drains, when applicable, must be routed separately from the downspouts and directly to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the approved point of subsurface discharge. Because these lines will all be routed to a combined sewer main, overflow from the non-infiltrating bioretention planters as well as the separate footing drains may join at a downstream catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer.  If footing drains are not proposed and/or required by another reviewer, please add a note on the DWC Plan that says, “Footing drains not proposed / required for this scope of work. ”  + WITH THIS, PLEASE ALSO UPDATE DWC PLAN NOTE #1D ACCORDINGLY.

Please complete and submit the following documents: 1) Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Soil Amendment  (CSC/SOIL) Plan 2) Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan 3) On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (Note: Because the proposed amount of new and replaced hard surface is more than 750 square feet, but less than 1500 square feet, only the "Project Information" and "Site Information" section of the Project Summary tab in the OSM Calculator must be completed. Subject: Seismic Site Class justification
Comment: The uploaded geotechnical report assumed Site Class D to determine seismic coefficients. To classify the site as Site Class D, please demonstrate one of the following criteria: a) Shear wave velocity for the top 100 ft is between 600 and 1,200 ft/s. b) SPT-N blow counts for the top 100 ft are between 15 and 50 per foot. c) Undrained shear strength for the top 100 ft is between 1,000 and 2,000 lb/ft². The subsurface explorations presented in the uploaded geotechnical report lack sufficient detail to determine the site class. As per Section 11.4.3 of ASCE 7-16, when soil properties are not known in sufficient detail to determine the site class, Site Class D is selected as the default site class, and the value of Fa shall not be less than 1.2. However, the uploaded structural calculations use an Fa value of 1.0. Please revise the seismic design parameters in the geotechnical report and update the structural design calculations accordingly.

Subject: Performance monitoring notes
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A. Please provide the shoring monitoring notes to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:  1) Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.  2) Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.   3) A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.  4) Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.  5) The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. Immediately and directly, notify SDCI and SDOT if any unusual or significantly increased movement occurs.  6) Immediately and directly notify the geotechnical and structural engineers, wall designer, SDCI, and SDOT if 0.5 inches of movement occurs between two consecutive readings and when total movements reach 0.5 inch. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team and SDOT (as indicated above).

Given this approach, please address the following: 1) On detail AFD/S1, the deeper wall/footing looks like a building foundation instead of a vault. Subject: 18 Foundations & Retaining Walls

Accordingly, the submitted excavation profile (that will be added to the drawings per the other current correction herein) shows the need for these walls to be installed with a footing drain.   Reviewer understands that drawing C02 shows the footing drains around all of the buildings, therefore as part of this revision record submit an updated drawing C02 that includes this vault footing drain.

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Comment: Sheet DWC: Please see below the requirements for projects with no off site point of stormwater discharge: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal: 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. Please note: Per  Appendix F, Section F-4 and Table F.11  of the Seattle Stormwater Manual, the HSPS Parameters must be modified based on the project site characteristics.  Please revise the  Pervious Land Segment (PERLND) and Impervious Land Segment (IMPLND) Runoff Parameters in the stormwater model as directed in the Manual.

Subject: 01 Administration
Comment: Informational for applicant on how to respond to city review comments: FOR INFORMATION ONLY.  In January 2022, SDCI transitioned to providing plan reviews via plan mark-up instead of traditional letters. We appreciate your understanding and patience as we rolled out the technology new to both applicants and SDCI staff.  The primary change that we are asking of applicants is that they document responses to comments directly in the plan set provided to them by SDCI at the end of each review cycle instead of sending letters corresponding to each correction letter. When all responses are documented, we ask that applicants upload the response plan set (as document type 'Correction Response Plan Set') along with the new, clean plan set as (document type 'Plan Set') for the next review cycle. This information is located at: https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/permits/how-to-respond-to-review-comments [If link is not active, cut and paste to URL] We have a video to help you learn how to navigate the new process here:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KB8laufkd7M. [If link is not active, cut and paste to URL] As we transition to delivering marked up plan sets, you may receive both letters and marked up plan sets with our corrections documented. As a rule, please respond to any marked-up plan set by embedding your responses in the marked-up plan set. We recognize that this transition requires changes to how you respond to our correction reports. We firmly believe that the changes we have instituted will lead to a reduction in the number of review cycles required to issue a permit. Remember, you will still: %ª Receive email notifications that a review has been completed. %ª Find review summary reports by discipline in the Seattle Services Portal as they are completed. %ª Updated plan sets can only be submitted after all reviews have been completed. What will be new is: %ª When all reviews are completed, you will receive a marked-up plan set which contains the comments from ALL the review disciplines. %ª Instead of preparing responses to each individual correction letter as you do today, you will be asked to reply to the comments directly in the marked-up plan set using either Bluebeam (requires a license) or Adobe Acrobat Reader (free).. %ª If you work with sub-consultants, you will need to coordinate with them to include their comments in your response plan set. Lastly, please help us perform reviews more efficiently! As we have worked on this transition, many of our reviewers indicated that they rely on bookmarks to navigate the (sometimes lengthy) plan sets that we receive from applicants. One thing that would allow us to review more quickly is to have applicants include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set that is submitted. Please follow the requirements for submitting pdf documents, outlined in Tip 106, General Standards for Plans and Drawings, [https://www.seattle.gov/DPD/Publications/CAM/cam106.pdf] to include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set you submit. NOTE: VERIFY THAT BOOKMARKS ARE NOT BROKEN PRIOR TO RESUBMITTING PLAN SETS. Bookmark links can become broken when sheets are added or removed from the plan set.01 Administration (2)

G022] Note, grade plane as defined by the SRC is not equivalent to average grade as defined by the Seattle Land Use Code. Grade plane may be established by calculating the average of the finish grade elevations at the major corners of the building or by considering the weighted average of the finish grade elevations at the perimeter of the building. Comment: Diaphragm continuity at stair openings and reentrant corners (building jogs) S2.X & ASCE 7 12.1.3 Calcs 52 At the continuous diaphragms with a garage, it appear that the calculations provide a rigid sub-diaphragm assumption for force distribution. This assumption relies on rotation of the garage diaphragm relative to the other parts of the structure. Per ASCE 7 12.1.3, sub parts of the structure are required to be attached. Clarify how continuity has been provided through the diaphragm (typically with strapping at reentrant corners). Response From Structural Engineer: The assumptions described are correct and the diaphragm is being rotated about the rest of the structure. Continuity has been provided per the continuous sheathing and members at the diaphragm interchange. Based on the low magnitude of the loads, this is adequate for transfer without the need for additional strapping. While this is defined as a re-entrant corner, it does not meet the requirements for an irregularity per ASCE Table 12.3-1, and therefore the forces do not need to be magnified per that requirement. Furthermore the wind beam and continuous double top plate at the stairs provides further continuity and load sharing between the diaphragms. Cycle 2 - Repeat comment The north side of the stair shear wall is not attached to the garage area or the living space to the east. Provide attachment to the diaphragm. The top plate is not continuous at this jogged corner. Similar an the south side of the garage.  SW202A is discontinuous at level 2 and the most direct load paths aro to either SW 103A, which has stair opening rendering the path not viable; or to SW101A, which would require a drag element to the east. Ev is the vertical seismic load effect and not a lateral force. Ensure that the directions of forces are properly accounted for in the design. Response From Structural Engineer: While the effects of Emh and Ev are in different directions, the overstrength design and load generations use equations directly from ASCE 12.4.3 to account for isolated vertical load effects on framing members below shearwalls. These effects are being calculated based on that section and are being properly accounted for in the design. Cycle 2 - This comment is made because the spreadsheet is incorrect and, nonconservative and can fail where h>l Repeat comment. Revise the spreadsheet to not add forces in different directions. The Emh is horizontal and applied to the top of the wall. Ev is vertical and applied as a distributed load through the wall. These forces shall never add. Please verify that this method was not used for the general shear wall overturning calculations.

Comment: Per Section D-2.3 of Appendix D of the Stormwater Manual, "Simple Subsurface Investigation", infiltration investigations during the Wet Season (November to March) shall demonstrate there is a minimum of 1 feet of separation between the bottom of the infiltration facility and a hydraulically restrictive layer or groundwater. According to the Simple Infiltration Checklist, the hole for the Subsurface Investigation was 4 feet deep.  The drywell shown on the plans has a depth of 4 feet of aggregate plus pavement on top.  The infiltration feasibility evaluation has not demonstrated that the minimum separation from groundwater or a hydraulically restrictive layer has been met. Also, the infiltration test was done at a depth of 3 feet.  It is recommended that the test hole depth be at the bottom of the facility to provide the best design information. Please provide documentation that complies with the Stormwater Manual requirements for determining infiltration feasibility.  See Section 3.2 of Volume 3 of the Seattle Stormwater Manual, "Determine Infiltration Feasibility".9 (6)

You are planning to work with the arborist to provide clearer documentation of the impacts to the doug fir and existing conditions. Language in the directors rule allows for removal of tier 2 trees if disturbance from construction will result in a non-viable tree: As part of a development permit application, trees that meet Tier 2 tree designation are not regulated as Tier 2 trees when SDCI finds that the tree should be removed based on a risk assessment produced by a registered tree service provider who is currently credentialed with an ISA Tree Risk Assessment Qualification. The risk assessment must document that the tree is considered a High Risk hazard or that the tree has little or no likelihood of survival after construction. In making this determination, the registered tree service provider must consider crown size, structure, disease, past maintenance practice, potential damage to existing or future targets, risk mitigation options, proposed demolition and construction methods, and the likelihood of survival after construction. Tree service providers conducting commercial tree work on these trees must comply with the tree service provider registry requirements of SMC Chapter 25.11 Subsection 25.11.100. The development impact area must include all areas on the site affected by proposed site improvements, site access, storage/stockpiling of materials, or construction activities such as grading, filling, trenching, or other excavation necessary to install utilities or access. Subject: General
Comment: DRAINAGE REVIEW APPEARS TO BE REQUIRED General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Additionally, single-family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must also implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference / when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  Please ensure that you are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates (when applicable and if not already included in the complete plan set) and/or standard plan notes.  Please note that even if drainage review is not required, a completed Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan is required to be included in the complete plan set when there is any ground disturbance.  As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable.  As part of the complete plan set, please submit the following: A completed Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan including the Site and Drainage Control Summary from On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator.  Insert in line with the Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan in the plan set. As a separate upload, please also submit a PDF of the entire completed On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator for review and retention. Without it, I cannot fully review or approve OSM BMP ’s.  Note: If On-site Stormwater Management is not required for the scope of the work, you do not have to submit a PDF of the OSM Calculator for review however, the Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator must still be completed and present on the DWC Plan as mentioned above leaving only the Infiltration and On-Site Stormwater Management sections at the bottom blank.Drainage (15)

Comment: If applicable, please clearly show and label the perimeter foundation/footing drain (FD or DRN) discharge lines being routed directly to and passing through a catch basin that meets the following requirements prior to connecting to the approved point of discharge as noted within this letter.  Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.E.1 “Water collected by subsurface drains shall pass through a catch basin before discharge to a public system or watercourse …”  See also, Table C in Section VII.D.   Catch basins for footing drains must have a 2 ’ deep minimum sump and a sump volume of 2 cubic feet. This must be clearly called out in the DWC Plan. Footing drains, when applicable, must be routed separately from the downspouts and directly to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer connection. Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.C.5 “In no case shall downspouts be connected directly to a groundwater collection system or the tight line connection from a groundwater collection system. ” On the DWC Plan, please show and label a separate foundation/footing drain collection line (if applicable) and a separate storm drain collection system.  Because these lines will all be routed to a combined sewer main, these collection lines may join at a downstream catch prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer.   If footing drains are not required and/or proposed with this scope of work, please add a prominent boxed note on the DWC Plan that says, “Footing drains are not required and/or proposed with this scope of work. ”

Subject: Subgrade and Bearing Pressure
Comment: (Revised and Repeated Item) SMC 22.170.110.A.1. Based on test pit logs presented in the Geotechnical report, dated June 26, 2024, competent bearing soils were generally encountered at about Elevation 231 feet, with the exception of northwest portion of the site. Test pits TP-2 and TP-3 in the southern portions of the site encountered up to 8 feet of LOOSE fill soils. Caving was observed in both of these two test pits, indicating a LOOSE condition.  However, based on plan sheets A1.00 and A1.02, the block walls are shown to bear on structural fill placed over up to 12 feet of LOOSE fill soils (based on information from test pits TP-2 and TP-3). In addition, some elevation views show additional weight (significant thickness of structural fill and structures) will be added to the slope, increasing the hazard of future earth movement given the underlying loose soil conditions. The ECA code requirement is that the proposed development meets complete stabilization. Upload an addendum to the geotechnical report that includes methods that demonstrate complete stabilization for the final grading condition, particularly on the southern project area. Include supporting calculations and evaluations to demonstrate complete stabilization in the addendum, and update the plan set accordingly.  SDCI reviewer will continue review in the next review cycle. ECA GeoTech (6)

Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.44 – Single-Family Residential
Comment: Partial Repeat Correction: The calculations provided on sheet A6/7 are incorrect. Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is a separate requirement from Gross Floor Area (GFA) allowance for DADUs. The plans do not propose a change to FAR since DADU structures are exempt from FAR per SMC 23.44.011. Remove the FAR calculations from the plans and replace with GFA calculations for the proposed DADU to demonstrate compliance with Table A for SMC 23.44.041 Letter f. Additionally, update the GFA calculations and diagrams to measure from the interior face of EXTERIOR WALLS. The area of shared interior walls between spaces that counts toward DADU GFA and space that does not count toward DADU GFA should be split between the two areas (i.e. half the interior wall between the storage area should be counted toward DADU GFA and the other half of the shared interior wall should not be counted. Same for shared garage wall).

Foundation ties:  Per ASCE 7-16 section 12.13.8.2: Individual pile caps, drilled piers, or caissons shall be interconnected by ties. Subject: DWC
Comment: Sheet DWC: Repeated correction: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer*. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*. *Note: for Infiltration testing and plan preparation clarification for detached accessory dwelling units (DADUs) and additions with less than 1,500 sf of new plus replaced hard surface on lots with No Off-site Point of Discharge:   The applicant is allowed to perform the infiltration testing unless otherwise determined by the Director.   If the applicant chooses (in lieu of a licensed professional) to conduct the infiltration testing, the applicant shall conduct the Small PIT (rather than the Simple Infiltration Test).   The test shall be documented with the Pilot Infiltration Test Checklist and a minimum 0.25 in/hr measured soil infiltration rate must be demonstrated.   Drywells shall be sized, at a minimum, per Appendix E-10 - Drywell Sizing Tables of the  Seattle Stormwater Manual.   The applicant is allowed to prepare the drainage control plan unless otherwise determined by the Director.Drainage (1)

Subject: Engineered Lateral
Comment: Outstanding Cycle 1 Comment: ASCE 7-16 12.1.2 - If using the dead loads that are within a light-framed shear wall to help reduce net uplift at the shear wall end, SDCI will accept using a tributary length of the shear wall that is the least of the following: a) half the total shear wall length; b) the shear wall height between stories; c) for FTAO or perforated shear wall, the distance from the shear wall end to midspan of the header of the nearest wall opening. Demonstrate that the portion of each shear wall assumed as contributing to resisting end uplift does not exceed this limit.  Alternatively, submit calculations justifying that the shear wall construction has adequate strength and rigidity to transfer dead loads from a greater tributary length. Additionally, it is unclear if appropriate load combinations are being used for calculation of overturning and resisting moments. Please revise shear wall calculations using the appropriate loads and load combinations for resisting overturning and provide holdowns as required.  Cycle 2 additional comments: Please provide a rational analysis demonstrating the shear walls act as rigid bodies for the purposes of transferring distributed dead load to the end of the wall and resiting overturning. SDCI agrees that this is an acceptable means of compliance, however calculations were not provided. The recommended dead load maximums are provided to not require rational analysis. Primary concern is walls with large openings, such as grid 1. Where multiple wall types utilize the same calculation, please provide a sample calculation for the worst case scenario describing load paths, demands and capacities to expedite review.Derek Ohlgren (4)

Subject: Engineered Lateral
Comment: Outstanding Cycle 1 comment: AWC SDPWS 4.3.2: The wood shearwalls appear to use the FTAO or perforated method for calculating shearwall capacity. Please provide these calculations instead of calculations based on overall wall length. Cycle 2 comment: FTAO calculations were not provided. Please provide calculations. A quick check of SW103A using the APA FTAO calculator indicated that panel edge nailing of 4" o.c. may be required.  FTAO may not be applicable for this wall due to the limited height above the window compromising the rigidity of the transfer panel. In the provided calculation (see snip at right) for SW 103A the total wall length of 11ft is used, with 8ft contributing. This is the appropriate value for the two individual qualifying wall piers. When individual piers are used a holdown is required at each pier. However the full length of the wall was used for the holdown calculation, indicating that FTAO was used for the shearwall calculation. FTAO typically requires additional nailing to transfer the forces around the opening. Please reconcile this difference and either provide a) holdowns at the end of each wall segment or b)increased nailing to meet the requirements of FTAO.

The risk assessment must document that the tree is considered a High Risk hazard or that the tree has little or no likelihood of survival after construction. Subject: Subgrade and bearing pressure
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A.1.  Based on subsurface information and recommendations presented in the geotechnical report by Riley Group dated January 31, 2025  as well as desired bottom of footing elevations, it appears that the eastern portion of the proposed development will be supported on footing founded where the loose silty sand was encountered in the exploration, B-1 up to 10 feet bgs. However, the geotechnical report recommended that the proposed structure be supported on conventional footings bearing on undisturbed soil, or on properly compacted structural fill. The geotechnical report further stated that the level 2 foundations that extend east requires loose soil overexcavation and backfilled with structural fill. Please revise the plan to include  (1) a foundation design and/or footing subgrade improvement that shows how the proposed development will be supported on the competent bearing soil and  (2) an excavation plan that shows extent and maximum cut slope conditions sufficient to expose competent bearing soil or elevation needed to improve footing subgrade that satisfies the recommendations presented in the geotechnical report.

Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Subject: General Tree Comment
Comment: CODES REVIEWED This project was reviewed for consistency with SMC 25.11, Tree Protection amended by Ordinance 126821. Depending on the information provided for review, additional correction cycles may result. Provide consistency across the plan set.    1. Based on available information, it does not appear that any excavation and/or construction-related activity will adversely impact any on- or off-site trees regulated by SMC 25.11. SDCI's standard tree and vegetation protection detail is not required to be shown in the plan set. Instead, please clearly note on all plan view sheets a defined "development impact area." The development impact area must include all areas on the site affected by proposed site improvements, site access, storage/stockpiling of materials, or construction activities such as grading, filling, trenching, or other excavation necessary to install utilities or access. The development impact area should encompass the area of the scope of work as well as the construction access and staging area, and it should be shown outside of tree driplines.  2. In addition to noting the development impact area in the plan set, include the following note on all plan view sheets: Tree Protection/Development Impact Area Requirements:   (1) Retention of all trees 6 inches or greater is required.   (2) No tree removal or damage is authorized.   (3) Construction-related activities, including excavation and ground disturbance, site access, heavy equipment use, storage, or stockpiling is prohibited outside of the development impact area unless located on existing hard surfaces. Comment: Flexible Diaphragm Shear Distribution - Wind Calcs 21 ASCE 7 12.3.1 ASCE 7 ch 26 definition: Diaphragm The wind load has been distributed to the wood sheathed and gyp sheathed shear walls. This is a flexible diaphragm, with shear loads attributed based on tributary area.  A) Clarify how tributary area was used to determine the interior gyp wall load. Note that it appears that an interior wall between edge walls should take half the total shear with a flexible diaphragm. In this case, with the slightly interior portal frame, it appears the interior gyp wall needs to take a bit less than half the wind shear. B) Provide a capacity vs demand calculation for the interior gyp walls. The portal frame is more than 6' from SW 103. At this and the level above the portal frame is a separate wall line in a flexible diaphragm. If it were in the same wall line, the loads would need to be distributed based on deflections, but the walls lines do not line up. C) Provide the flexible diaphragm shear distribution showing how the loads were assigned to the portal frame and all walls in the EW direction.
